english_translation: Two guests (at the same time) have no welcome.

kikuyu_text: Aka matiri cia ndiiro no cia nyiniko
english_translation: Women have no upright words, but only crooked ones The Kikuyu use the proverb to say that women keep no secrets and seldom tell the truth.
cultural_meaning: Women conceal all that they know not

english_translation: Men do not know liberality One does not give without hope of return
Me do not know hard firewood, but only lops people put aside hard tasks and devote themselves only to easy ones.
The elders drink afterwards (i.e after the others) Elderly people are not in such a hurry as young ones.
He who spends his time adorning himself knows he is going to a dance There is a reason for everything
A secret agreement enabled people to kill Watatua Watatua was a powerful Chief, invincible in open combat, who was killed at night by a few men
cultural_meaning: Secret union means strength.

english_translation: One appointment is eatedn by another Today kills yesterday.
Lying is the thief’s stronghold.

kikuyu_text: Guciara uru ti kwenda kwa mwene
english_translation: It is not the mother’s will to have a bad offspring.
The fact that you have gone near the battle-field does not mean that you fought.
Thieves conceal themselves in the night not in the day. The night is a cloak for sinners.
Travelling teaches men their way.
There is no difference between the thief and the looker-on.
Nobody entering a hut pays for the heart he will enjoy in it. Only the owner of the hut had the drudgery of carrying home the firewood; the
cultural_meaning: visitor does not know the cost of the fire he is enjoying. Metaphorically the proverb is used to say that he who enters a house cannot realise the troubles of the occupants. None knows the weight of another’s burden.

english_translation: No prepotent man will insult other people for two consecutive seasons. Prepotence comes quickly to an end.
Nobody walks with another man’s gait. Every man in his way.
The day is for working, the night is for resting. There is a time to wink as well as to see.
A good action reaps another One good turn deserves another
The good milking cow is praised after her death A friend is never known till needed.
The ox that claws the ‘kiara’ will die. ‘Kiara’ is the dunghill you will find in every Kikuyu village. In order to understand the proverb it much be borne in mind that the Kikuyu
cultural_meaning: regard it as a sacred place which the witch-doctors dedicates with the sacrifice of a goat to secure that the evil spirits may not return into the hut from which he expelled them. They are supposed to stay in the ‘kiara’ just as the rubbish does Touch pitch and you’ll be defiled.

english_translation: The ox that feeds itself does not spoil its skin.
The ox which has no horns, relies for help on the one that has them He who feels weak relies on the friend he knows is strong.
The tooth laughs with the lance. It means that oftern a person plays with his enemy. The cat plays with the mouse
Young suga-cane gives no beer There is no putting old heads on young shoulders.
The foot and the earth cannot help meeting.
Candidates for circumcision 0 after washing do not return to warm themselves at their father’s (but go straightaway to the place of the ceremony to show their courage)
cultural_meaning: In things that must be it is good to be resolute.

english_translation: The pit allows the grass to fall in The proverb alludes to the pits the Kikuyu used to dig for trapping wild animals. These pits were covered with sticks over which, as well as
cultural_meaning: over borders, they put a layer of grass. Since this grass often fell in the pit through the spaces between the sticks, so they say that often one falls into the pit dug by himself. Hoist with his own petard.

english_translation: The hunter’s son knows how to hunt Like father, like son.

kikuyu_text: Kahiu karathime kariaga nyama cia kinandu
english_translation: The blessed knife (son) eats of the meat of the ‘kinandu’ ‘Kinandu’ is a small calabash used to keep oil, fat and the best morsels of meat. They say that the father share the contents of the ‘kinandu’
cultural_meaning: with the most beloved son.

english_translation: The fed baby plays on its mother’s bed
The rambling pole-cat leaves its house when there is banquet. The son that leaves his father’s house for liberty’s sake will not share his father’s inheritance
A little idleness lost a tilled field A little leak can sink a great ship
The food eaten first lasts longest in the stomach First impressions are most lasting.

kikuyu_text: Kindu kiuru no kironda, indi kiri rua rwa muhuhi
english_translation: Literal translation: A sore is a really bad thing; still it means luck to the doctor.
english_equivalent: It is an ill wind that blows nobody good.

kikuyu_text: Kiriro kiri ituura gitingireka mundu akome
english_translation: Literal translation: One person weeping prevents all in a village from sleeping.
english_equivalent: One barking dog sets all the street a-barking.

kikuyu_text: Kirimu kihithaga rwembea-ini rwa nyumba kiui gitikuonwo
english_translation: Literal translation: The fool hides himself under the eaves of the hut and thinks nobody will see him.
cultural_meaning: It refers to foolish people who invent silly excuses to conceal their faults.

kikuyu_text: Kirimu gia gwikigia kirugite kia muciarire
english_translation: Literal translation: He who feigns to be stupid is more stupid than the stupid-born.
english_equivalent: None is so deaf as those who won’t hear.

english_translation: Literal translation: A fool is like a beehive.
cultural_meaning: The proverb means that he is a fool who does not look after his own interest, like the beehive which allows itsself to be emptied.

english_translation: Literal translation: Desires tie.
english_equivalent: If desire be endless, your cares will be so too.

english_translation: Literal translation: An empty bowl is not offered.
cultural_meaning: It means that it is better to keep silence than to try to justify oneself by empty excuses.
english_equivalent: Be silent or speak something worth hearing.

english_translation: Literal translation: Knowing too much is like being ignorant.
english_equivalent: Too much breaks the bag.

english_translation: Literal translation: To be caught is not to be imrisoned.
english_equivalent: There is many a slip, ‘twixt the cup and the lip.

english_translation: Literal translation: One cannot put the ‘ndebe’ into a broken ear-lobe. done with a wooden bodkin by the parents of the boy or girl in the years preceding the initiation. Pieces of wood are then introduced into
cultural_meaning: the hole and these will successively be replaced by larger ones until a large wooden ring (‘ndebe’) can be put in as an ornament. The proverb means that these are things once broken cannot be soldered.
english_equivalent: ‘Ndebe’ is the wooden ring put into the pierced ear-lobe as an ornament. The painful operation of piercing the lobe is

english_translation: Literal translation: Not all days are sundays.
english_equivalent: Christmas comes but once in a year.

kikuyu_text: Mugunda wa mwere umenyagwo na ngetho
english_translation: Literal translation: One knows a field of millet from its crop.
english_equivalent: A tree is known by its fruits.

english_translation: Literal translation: A woman that hangs about does not lack children.
cultural_meaning: The proverb refers to the married women who, failing to have children of their husbands’, go around looking for other men.

kikuyu_text: Mura na mundu ti mura na hiti
english_translation: Literal translation: To be robbed by a person is different from being robbed by a hyena.
cultural_meaning: The proverb means that if you were robbed by a person, you can hope to be recompensed for the damage; but if a member of your family or a head of your herd has been stoled by a hyena, there is no hope for redress.
english_equivalent: There are injuries beyond redress.

english_translation: Literal translation: One must not break the arm of him who tills the fields.
english_equivalent: Do not kill the goose that lays the golden eggs.

english_translation: Literal translation: One tiller does not fill the granary.
english_equivalent: Union is strength.

kikuyu_text: Muthakwa wa athi nduthiragwo ni gicanjara
english_translation: Literal translation: The ‘muthakwa-tree’ will not discontinue to produce branches of only one shape.
english_equivalent: Like father like son.

kikuyu_text: Muthuri utari kahii niwe wiriragira ngururu
english_translation: Literal translation: The married man who has no son goes himself to scare away the birds from his harvest.

kikuyu_text: Mutirima wa kirimu witirimagia na mugi
english_translation: Literal translation: A fool’s walking-stick helps the wise man to stand.
cultural_meaning: This proverb means that wise people know how to get profit from things that a man thinks useless.
english_equivalent: A wise man gets learning from those who have none themselves.

kikuyu_text: Mutumia na kionje ni undu umwe.
english_translation: Literal translation: A woman and an invalid man are the same thing.
english_equivalent: Words for women, actions for men.

english_translation: Literal translation: The son of sin does not cease weeping.
english_equivalent: Sin and debts are always more than we think them to be.

english_translation: Literal translation: He who airs something must air himself first.
english_equivalent: No gains without pains.

kikuyu_text: Nda imwe yumaga muici na murogi
english_translation: Literal translation: The same womb gives birth to a thief and a poisoner.
Literal translation: The long road arrives (at the goal).
cultural_meaning: The proverb means that a long but sure way, is better than a short but dangerous one.
english_equivalent: Fair and softly goes far in a day.

english_translation: Literal translation: The ox does not become old with strong muscles.
cultural_meaning: The proverb means that man cannot expect to age and retain the vigour of his youth.

english_translation: Literal translation: Every little hole of the ear has its little thorn.
cultural_meaning: The Kikuyu used to put little sticks or thorns in the pierced upper part of the ear.
english_equivalent: Every sparrow to its ear of wheat.

kikuyu_text: Ngware ikirara muti iguru ndiatigire thi kuri kwega
english_translation: Literal translation: The francolin sleeps on a tree because it is not all right on the ground (and on a tree it feels safer).
english_equivalent: Everyone knows his business best.

english_translation: Literal translation: A strong man is not overpowered by his task.
english_equivalent: He that endures is not overcome.

english_translation: Literal translation: Woman, remember that the mouth is sometimes covered with a branch.
english_equivalent: A woman cannot keep a secret.

english_translation: Literal translation: Beauty does no good.
english_equivalent: Beauty may have fair leaves, yet bitter fruit.

english_translation: Literal translation: The food one takes as provision for one’s journey is not carried by another person.
english_equivalent: Take heed is a good read.

english_translation: Literal translation: The watering eye makes the nose water.
english_equivalent: When the head aches all the body is the worse.

english_translation: Literal translation: A tree branch cannot put forth a man.
english_equivalent: Nothing comes out of the sack but what was in it.

kikuyu_text: Thiga ni muruu: marara nja gutiri
english_translation: Literal translation: ‘Thiga’ is circumcissed: there is no reward in passing the night in the courtyard.
cultural_meaning: ‘Thiga’ means a certain fellow. The proverb originates in one of the many customs relating to the Kikuyu ceremony of circumcission. On the eve of the circumcission day women and girls gather at the hut of the candidate and sing for a great part in the night; not gratuitously, but in the hope of getting food and beer from the candidates mother. But if when the rite is completed, she makes as an excuse that now the child is circumcissed and refuses to give them what they expect, they start singing the above strain, meaning: ‘Have no recourse to the idle pretext that your son is now circumcissed; but rather give us the reward to which we are entitled after a night’s singing and dancing’.
english_equivalent: Eaten bread is soon forgotten.

english_translation: Literal translation: The duiker cannot help panting.
english_equivalent: The leopard cannot change his spots.

english_translation: Literal translation: Choose between dying and living; i.e. between death and life, war and peace.
Literal translation: Where men have passed there is not a single feather to pick up.
Literal translation: The man who has a family does not adorn his family with finery.
english_equivalent: Children are certain cares, but uncertain comforts.

english_translation: Literal translation: The tilling does not come to an end.
Literal translation: One hates to see the blood of a thing that belongs to him.
cultural_meaning: The proverb means that one’s heart is affected by the pains of the persons and animals whom one loves.
english_equivalent: Whom we love best, them we want to be happy.

english_translation: Literal translation: The open place where men used to stay cannot help stinking (because of the many quarrels and thefts which occur
cultural_meaning: therein).
